reddit_58.response:
To be honest, my perception of DBS leadership hasn’t shifted from "skeptical" to "convinced"—if anything, it’s shifted toward "exhausted." While some see a CEO replying on LinkedIn as a sign of radical transparency, as a freelancer who lives and dies by my cash flow, it feels like watching a high-budget PR performance while my own stage is falling apart.

*   The CEO’s intervention feels like a "digital band-aid" on a structural wound. Two weeks later, the LinkedIn post has been buried by the algorithm, but the underlying anxiety for people like me remains. For the bank, a system error is a line item in a risk report; for me, it’s the difference between paying my subcontractors on time or losing my professional reputation. Seeing a polished response to a viral complaint doesn't give me more confidence in the server stability; it just tells me that you have to be "loud" on social media to get the leadership’s attention.

*   Operational reliability isn’t something you can fix with a comment thread. My perception of the bank's reliability is shaped by the spinning wheel on the Digibank app at 2:00 AM when I’m trying to verify a client’s deposit. In the two weeks since that interaction, I haven’t seen a roadmap for technical redundancy; I’ve only seen a masterclass in crisis management. If the leadership spent as much energy on legacy system migration as they do on personal branding, maybe we wouldn't have to worry every time there’s a "scheduled maintenance."

*   There is a massive disconnect between the "bank of the future" narrative and the "survival of the present" reality. I’ve observed that the interaction focused heavily on the optics of empathy, but for the "invisible" users—the freelancers and small vendors who don't have 10,000 LinkedIn followers—we are still stuck with automated chatbots and generic "we apologize for the inconvenience" emails. The CEO’s intervention felt like a "VIP lane" for a public relations crisis, which actually makes me trust the system *less* because it suggests that the squeaky wheel gets the grease, while the rest of us just get the friction.

*   I’m tired of hearing about "digital transformation" when the human cost of a downtime event is so high. Your record-breaking profits don't mean anything to me if I can't access my own money to pay rent during a glitch. Two weeks later, my stance is clear: I don't need a "relatable" CEO; I need a boring, invisible, and 100% functional banking utility. Until the outages stop for good, the LinkedIn activity is just noise that distracts from the fact that our livelihoods are being treated as collateral for your "learning curve."

While Tan Su Shan’s direct engagement shows a certain level of accountability at the top, leadership for me isn’t measured by the ability to reply to a post; it’s measured by whether that reply translates into a 100% uptime for the systems my clients rely on.

*   From my perspective as a real estate agent, the CEO’s intervention feels like a "social mask" for the bank. It’s a nice gesture, but it doesn’t address the core issue of transaction certainty. If a client is at a showflat and the banking app fails during the transfer of an Option Fee, a LinkedIn comment won't save that deal from falling through... 💼

*   My assessment of operational reliability hasn’t improved because we haven’t seen a transparent update on the SLA (Service Level Agreement) or structural changes to the backend infrastructure. In this industry, we operate on tight timelines—especially with ABSD deadlines and completion dates. Any lag in the system is a risk to my clients' capital and my professional reputation.

*   The simulation of public sentiment over these two weeks has shown a lot of "likes," but very little talk about technical redundancy. I’ve noticed that while the "Netizen Critics" are temporarily silenced by the CEO’s presence, the professional community is still waiting for evidence that the "bureaucratic lag" mentioned in the feedback is being dismantled.

*   I am still haunted by the memory of a client almost losing five figures because an OTP deposit was delayed by "system maintenance" that wasn't properly communicated. Seeing a CEO reply to one individual doesn't give me the assurance that the next time my client needs to move significant funds for a property settlement, the pipes will actually work... 📉

*   Leadership is about systemic reliability, not individual firefighting. Two weeks later, I still see a bank that is very good at crisis communication but hasn't yet proven it has solved the technical debt that leads to these service disruptions in the first place. Until I see a quarter without a major "OTP" or transfer glitch, my stance remains highly critical.
